numerical_failure.observed_behavior: VIF values explode to extremely high numbers (e.g., 20, 40, 60, 100+), and in the precision edge-case can become inf due to division by zero with a “zero division warning”; in other cases they become very large finite values instead of inf (e.g., vif=1e14, 1e20, 1e200).
numerical_failure.expected_behavior: VIF should not explode unrealistically when there is no real multicollinearity; numerical computation should yield stable, accurate VIF values (no unnecessary explosion to 20/40/60/100+; and avoiding inf caused by floating-point precision where the instability is not due to true collinearity).
trigger_conditions: Computing VIF via auxiliary regression R-squared and converting using vif = 1 / (1 - r_squared_i); when r_squared_i is close enough to 1 that (1 - rsquared) becomes exactly zero in floating-point, leading to division by zero (inf plus zero division warning).

When the design matrix includes monotonic nonlinear transformations—especially 1/x, log(x), 1/y, log(y)—in datasets that otherwise have no real multicollinearity among independent variables, causing exploding VIF values.

Mixing columns with wildly different numeric ranges (e.g., huge numbers with tiny fractions alongside a column of 1s), which makes regression math snowball rounding mistakes into wrong VIF values; standardizing (rescaling columns to same scale) prevents the instability.
Use of very small ridge_factor in the context mentioned in #2380 can make vif=inf (singular) become very large but finite; the instability is numerical.

input_output_examples.input: Design matrix includes common econometric transformations such as 1/x and log(x) (monotonic nonlinear transformations), despite no real multicollinearity among independent variables.
input_output_examples.buggy_output: VIF values explode to extremely high numbers (20, 40, 60, 100+).
input_output_examples.expected_output: VIF values should remain stable and not indicate severe multicollinearity when there is none.

input_output_examples.input: Computation uses vif = 1. / (1. - r_squared_i) where floating point precision makes (1-rsquared) exactly equal to zero.
input_output_examples.buggy_output: vif = inf with zero division warning.
input_output_examples.expected_output: Instead of inf from zero division caused by floating-point precision, VIF should be very large finite values reflecting the numerical instability context or otherwise computed without triggering the exact zero denominator; the PR notes using ssr/tss (unexplained fraction) avoids this precision issue.

input_output_examples.input: Same precision edge-case, but consequence described as small-denominator numerical noise producing very large finite VIF instead of inf.
input_output_examples.buggy_output: vif values can be very large finite numbers such as 1e14, 1e20, 1e200.
input_output_examples.expected_output: More appropriate behavior is that these correspond to near-collinearity numerically but should not manifest as an unrealistic explosion or inf purely due to floating-point rounding; using ssr/tss keeps the denominator around small values rather than producing an exact zero from 1-r_squared.

oracle_clues: Numerical precision issue specifically identified: vif = 1/(1 - r_squared_i) can make (1-rsquared) exactly zero in floating point, leading to inf with zero division warning.
Alternative computation mentioned as oracle clue: use ssr / tss instead of (1 - r_squared), so the denominator can be very small without hitting exact zero caused by floating point near 1.

Oracle clue for correctness: With standardize=True, VIFs stay stable and no warnings appear; with standardize=False on bad transformed data, warnings fire and VIFs break as expected (PR#9835 added test_vif_instability).
Magnitude oracle clue from ISSUE #9791: VIF values explode to 20, 40, 60, 100+ even when there is no real multicollinearity.

numerical_characteristics.precision: floating point precision makes `(1-rsquared)` exactly equal to zero, causing `vif` to become `inf` with a zero division warning; also mentions floating point around zero instead of floating point around 1 when using alternative denominators
numerical_characteristics.magnitude: VIF can become `inf` (in the failure mode), or very large finite values such as `1e14`, `1e20`, `1e200`; similarly, small ridge_factor can make `vif=inf (singulat)` instead become very large but finite
category_specific_evidence: Bug in `variance_inflation_factor`: it computes `vif = 1. / (1. - r_squared_i)` using `rsquared` from an auxiliary regression (ISSUE #6251).
Failure mode: for small `r_squared`, floating point precision makes `(1-rsquared)` exactly equal to zero, so `vif` becomes `inf` with a zero division warning (ISSUE #6251).

Mathematical/denominator property involved: the reciprocal transformation `1/(1-r_squared)` becomes numerically unstable when `1-r_squared` underflows to exactly zero; the proposed alternative uses the unexplained fraction (ISSUE #6251): use `ssr / tss` instead of `(1-r_squared)` so the denominator is small around zero rather than `1-r_squared` around one (description in ISSUE #6251).
Consequence statement: in many cases this yields very large finite VIF instead of `vif=Inf` (ISSUE #6251), with example magnitudes `vif=1e14 or 1e20 or 1e200` (ISSUE #6251).
Fix description: PR #9835 clips `r_sq` before computing `1/(1-r_sq)` in `variance_inflation_factor` (issue#6251; ISSUE #6251).

Test evidence: `test_diff:...` asserts standardize=True and standardize=False match closely on clean, well-conditioned data, using `assert_allclose(vif_true, vif_false, rtol=1e-7)` (test_influence.py:331-367).
reproduction_risks: Reproduction may require data that yields very small `r_squared` so that `1-rsquared` underflows to exactly zero; otherwise the error may only show up as very large finite VIF rather than `inf`.
If data is only 'nearly' singular/collinear, reproduction might produce large finite values (e.g., `1e14`, `1e20`, `1e200`) instead of `inf`, depending on conditioning.
The fix involves clipping `r_sq` (PR #9835), so reproducing on a branch with the fix may not show the original `inf`/zero-division behavior.
